text: Red and blue can only have a useful real-time conversation if they're both talking about the exact same thing. That shared vocabulary comes from the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and this lesson covers how to map every attacker action to it live, during the exercise itself, not afterward in a report.

ATT&CK organizes real adversary behavior around fourteen tactics — the attacker's goal at a given stage, like Initial Access, Privilege Escalation, or Exfiltration. Underneath each tactic sit techniques, and often sub-techniques, each with a stable ID: T1059 is Command and Scripting Interpreter, and T1059.001 is specifically PowerShell. That same ID means the same thing in a threat intel report, in red's own notes, and in blue's detection coverage matrix.

That's why red announces the ID, not just a description. Saying 'T1003.001, LSASS memory dumping, under Credential Access' is unambiguous in a way that 'trying to grab some passwords' never is. Because blue's own coverage matrix is organized by the same IDs, hearing the exact technique number lets them instantly check whether a rule covering that specific behavior is supposed to exist, instead of guessing which detection might apply.

The MITRE ATT&CK Navigator, a free tool, turns that into something visual. It renders the whole matrix as a grid, and during the exercise the scribe marks each tested technique green for detected cleanly, yellow for detected but slow or noisy, and red for not detected at all. By the end of the session, the room is looking at an actual heat map of real coverage, not a list buried in a spreadsheet.

Because ATT&CK also documents specific known threat groups and the exact techniques they've been observed using, mapping your results to the same IDs lets you ask a sharper question than whether you tested a few things. You can ask how many of a specific ransomware group's recently observed techniques your environment actually detects today — and that comparison is only possible because everything is tracked against the same shared IDs.

Mapping gives the exercise its shared language and its heat map. What happens next is the whole point of doing any of this: turning every gap that map reveals into an actual, tuned detection rule running in production. That's where the next lesson picks up.
